body:
Why biotechnology needs different regulators

Biotechnology products can involve different types of risk. A genetically engineered organism released into the environment raises questions about ecological safety. A vaccine raises questions about its quality, safety and effectiveness in people. A biofertiliser raises questions about microbial identity and product quality.

India therefore uses different laws and regulatory bodies according to the activity and product involved. The fact that a product uses biotechnology does not place every aspect of its regulation under a single authority.

Regulation of genetically engineered organisms

The principal framework for genetically engineered organisms and certain hazardous microorganisms is the 1989 Rules issued under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. These rules establish responsibilities for biosafety review and oversight.

Three bodies are especially important for school-level and prelims preparation.

BodyInstitutional associationMain function
IBSC — Institutional Biosafety CommitteeInstitution undertaking relevant researchInstitution-level biosafety oversight
RCGM — Review Committee on Genetic ManipulationDepartment of BiotechnologySafety oversight of relevant ongoing genetic-engineering research
GEAC — Genetic Engineering Appraisal CommitteeMinistry of Environment, Forest and Climate ChangeEnvironmental appraisal of large-scale activities and proposed environmental release of genetically engineered organisms

The role of GEAC

The Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee (GEAC) functions under the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC). It appraises proposals involving environmental release of genetically engineered organisms, including relevant experimental field trials, and specified large-scale uses of hazardous microorganisms and recombinant organisms.

In the context of a genetically modified crop, biosafety assessment and environmental appraisal are central concerns. A favourable assessment for a particular activity is not equivalent to unrestricted permission for every use of that organism.

The correct expansion is Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee. It should not be confused with an agricultural research institution, a pharmaceutical regulator or the state biotechnology mission.

Regulation of medicines and vaccines

The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) is India's central drug regulatory organisation, functioning under the Directorate General of Health Services, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. The Drugs Controller General of India (DCGI) performs central regulatory functions that include approval of new drugs and specified product licences, including vaccines.

The principal legal framework includes the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, and the applicable rules. The New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019, are relevant to the approval and study of new drugs and vaccines.

State drug-control authorities, including Gujarat's Food and Drugs Control Administration (FDCA), carry out important functions concerning drug manufacturing, sale, distribution and enforcement within their assigned jurisdiction. Central approval of a new drug and state-level regulatory functions are related but distinct.

A biotechnology research organisation or a state industrial-promotion agency cannot substitute its recommendation for the legally required drug-regulatory permission.

Biofertilisers, biopesticides and food products

Other biotechnology-related agricultural and food products have different regulatory frameworks:

  • Biofertilisers: Product standards for notified biofertilisers are addressed under the Fertiliser (Control) Order, 1985. The emphasis includes the identity and quality of the beneficial microbial product.
  • Biopesticides: Applicable biopesticide registration is governed by the Insecticides Act, 1968, and related rules, involving the Central Insecticides Board and Registration Committee (CIB&RC) framework.
  • Food products: The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has responsibilities under India's food-safety framework. Food-product requirements must not be confused with environmental permission to release a genetically engineered organism.

These distinctions are important because a genetically modified crop, a microbial pesticide and a microbial fertiliser may all involve biotechnology but have different intended uses and regulatory requirements.

Gujarat's development agencies are not statutory substitutes

GSBTM may promote biotechnology, GBRC may undertake research, GBU may train biotechnology professionals, and STBI may support product development. None of these functions, by itself, grants the manufacturer permission to release a genetically modified crop into the environment or market an unapproved vaccine.

Likewise, industrial facilities must comply with applicable environmental and pollution-control requirements. In Gujarat, the Gujarat Pollution Control Board (GPCB) is relevant to environmental compliance; it is not a replacement for medicine or genetic-engineering regulators.

Approval is activity-specific. Research permission, environmental release, clinical trials, medicine manufacturing, pesticide registration and food safety may involve different legal requirements. Approval for one purpose must not be assumed to authorise every other purpose.

Prelims focus

  • The 1989 Rules on genetically engineered organisms operate under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.
  • RCGM is associated with the Department of Biotechnology; GEAC with MoEFCC.
  • CDSCO and DCGI are associated with drug and vaccine regulation.
  • The Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, and New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019, are important for medicines and vaccines.
  • The Fertiliser (Control) Order, 1985, covers notified biofertiliser standards; the Insecticides Act, 1968, is relevant to biopesticides.
  • Trap: GEAC is not India's general authority for approving every biotechnology medicine or vaccine.

[Department of Biotechnology, Indian Biosafety Knowledge Portal, Committees and RCGM Procedures, official website consulted 13 November 2026; Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee, About GEAC and Functions, MoEFCC, official website consulted 13 November 2026; Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation, Functions, official website consulted 13 November 2026; Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare, Use of Bio-Fertilisers, 7 February 2023; Directorate of Plant Protection, Quarantine and Storage, Checklist for Registration of Biopesticides under the Insecticides Act, 1968, sections 9(3B) and 9(3), official document consulted 13 November 2026; Savli Technology and Business Incubator, Facilities and Amenities, official website consulted 13 November 2026.]

title: Biotechnology Regulation in India: Biosafety, Drug Approval and Agricultural Products

body:
The policy and its period

The Government of Gujarat issued the Gujarat State Biotechnology (BT) Policy 2022–27 through Government Resolution BTP/022022/446/BT dated 15 February 2022. It is a state policy intended to encourage biotechnology research, enterprises, manufacturing, investment and skilled employment.

The policy builds upon the state's pharmaceutical and industrial strengths while promoting biotechnology applications in healthcare, agriculture, industry, environmental management and biological services.

As of the selected content cutoff, 13 November 2026, Gujarat's Department of Science and Technology and its incentive portal continued to publish and administer the 2022–27 policy. Statements describing its objectives and financial assistance should be understood in that policy context.

Official 5-year targets

The policy sets out the following targets for its intended 5-year period.

MeasurePolicy targetCorrect interpretation
Biotechnology units and businessesSupport at least 500Target for support
InvestmentMore than INR 20,000 croreTarget for investment attraction
EmploymentMore than 120,000 jobsTarget for employment creation

These are policy targets announced in 2022. They are not verified figures for actual investments received, companies established or employment achieved by November 2026. When a question asks for the target, use the announced target; when it asks for the actual achievement, a separate dated performance report is necessary.

What kinds of activities can the policy support?

The policy defines a wide range of biotechnology products, processes and services. Its listed areas include vaccines, recombinant therapeutic products, molecular diagnostics, biofertilisers, biopesticides, bioplastics, biofuels, tissue culture, fermentation, genomics and bioinformatics.

This wide coverage reflects the fact that biotechnology is not confined to medical manufacturing. A biotechnology enterprise may produce a microbial agricultural input, develop a diagnostic service, manufacture an enzyme or pursue vaccine-related research.

Industrial development and infrastructure

The policy seeks to strengthen the environment in which biotechnology enterprises operate. Important measures include support for specialised infrastructure, access to research facilities, start-up development and manufacturing investment.

The policy identifies institutions and facilities such as GBU, GBRC, the Savli biotechnology cluster and STBI. It also refers to the Gujarat Biotech Start-Up Venture Fund (GBSVF) as a venture-financing initiative associated with the state's biotechnology development efforts.

Infrastructure and venture financing serve different purposes. A shared laboratory allows access to scientific facilities; an incubator supports developing enterprises; investment assistance helps eligible industrial units meet specified costs; venture financing provides capital through investment arrangements rather than constituting a product-safety permission.

Important policy definitions and assistance

The policy uses the term gross fixed capital investment (GFCI) for qualifying investment in fixed assets associated with a biotechnology unit. Its definition excludes land cost. It also distinguishes GFCI from eligible GFCI (eGFCI): building expenditure cannot exceed 20% of eGFCI, and expenditure on movable items such as computers and software, furniture and fixtures, office equipment and vehicles is excluded.

For classification as a mega project, the policy specifies an eligible biotechnology unit with either GFCI of at least INR 200 crore or direct employment of at least 500 people. The word or is important: meeting either stated condition satisfies this classification criterion.

For the policy's Package 1, covering specified eligible units with GFCI below INR 200 crore, the announced capital-assistance provision is 25% of eligible GFCI, subject to a ceiling of INR 40 crore. The policy also describes operational assistance at 15% of eligible operational expenditure, subject to a ceiling of INR 5 crore per year. These are scheme provisions, not unconditional payments to every biotechnology business; applicants must satisfy the relevant definitions, eligibility requirements and implementation conditions.

Separate 3 kinds of policy information: a target states what the government aims to achieve; an eligibility criterion states who may qualify; an incentive provision states what assistance may be available to an eligible applicant. None of these, on its own, proves that a specific company received money or that the policy target was achieved.

Connecting the policy with actual biotechnology applications

Consider 3 different proposals. A company developing a microbial biofertiliser falls within agricultural biotechnology. A company developing recombinant insulin falls within biopharmaceutical biotechnology. An enterprise offering genome-sequencing analysis falls within biotechnology services.

All 3 may be relevant to Gujarat's biotechnology policy, subject to its actual definitions and conditions. Their regulatory pathways nevertheless differ because the resulting products and activities are different.

One-glance understanding of Gujarat's biotechnology ecosystem

The simplest way to understand the whole subject is to distinguish science, institutions, applications and regulation.

  • Science: microorganisms, DNA, genes, enzymes, cell culture and genomics provide the biological foundation.
  • Institutions: GSBTM supports sector development; GBRC undertakes research; GBU provides education and research; STBI supports start-ups; the Savli park initiative concerns industrial infrastructure.
  • Applications: vaccines, therapeutic proteins, Bt cotton, biofertilisers, industrial fermentation, biogas and molecular diagnostics meet different practical needs.
  • Regulation: GEAC examines relevant environmental-release proposals; CDSCO and DCGI perform central drug-regulatory functions; other authorities govern applicable agricultural inputs and food products.

Knowing which category an institution or product belongs to makes factual matching and statement-based reasoning more reliable. The central question is always whether a statement concerns research, manufacturing, policy support, environmental safety, medicine approval or agricultural-product regulation.

Prelims focus

  • Gujarat State Biotechnology Policy 2022–27 was issued on 15 February 2022.
  • The 5-year targets include at least 500 supported units, more than INR 20,000 crore of investment and more than 120,000 jobs.
  • A mega biotechnology project meets the policy criterion of at least INR 200 crore GFCI or at least 500 direct jobs.
  • Package 1 states capital assistance of 25% of eligible GFCI, capped at INR 40 crore, subject to applicable conditions.
  • GBSVF is associated with biotechnology start-up venture financing, not product approval.
  • Trap: Announced policy targets must not be presented as achieved results.

[Government of Gujarat, Gujarat State Biotechnology (BT) Policy 2022–27, Government Resolution BTP/022022/446/BT dated 15 February 2022, sections 3.1, 4.4, 5.2, 5.8–5.11, 6 and 7, pp. 3–12; Gujarat State Biotechnology Mission, Government Resolutions, entry dated 15 February 2022; Gujarat Department of Science and Technology, Incentive Management Portal, Biotechnology Policy 2022–27 and Application Guidelines, consulted 13 November 2026.]
